newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks slide, dollar rises to 46-month high.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks slide, dollar rises to 46-month high.

text.p: Japanese stocks skidded sharply lower on Monday, led by a futures sell-off said to signal market disapproval of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's economic policies due to be outlined later in the day.

"The selling of futures contracts means the market thinks there is little for it to look forward to in the coming months, although parliament is starting today," said Tadahiro Kamogawa, general manager at Yamaichi Securities.
Some market participants bought futures late last week on hopes that the government would try to rescue the stock market once parliament opened on Monday, traders said.
But hope of any good news from the parliamentary session, which convenes later on Monday, seemed to be fading.
"Everyone was hoping that something good for the stock market will come out of parliament, but some are beginning to think otherwise," said a broker at one of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages.
The 225-share Nikkei averaged opened a tad higher, but soon succumbed to waves of unwinding of arbitrage-linked positions in morning trading.

By midday it had lost 466.36 points, or 2.58 percent, to close the morning session at 17,623.68. March futures contracts were down 520 points at 17,610. At the start of afternoon trading, the Nikkei extended its slide to more than 500 points.
The dollar, meanwhile, rose to a fresh 46-month high against the yen of 117.67 yen in morning trade, as the stock market slide prompted yen selling by overseas operators.
The Nikkei plunged more than 2,000 points in the first trading week of this year on worries that Japan's tentative economic recovery may falter in the face of a planned fiscal tightening.
It recovered some ground last week but participants were anxious to see if the government would offer it any concrete support in the new parliamentary session.

Hashimoto was due to make a keynote address to the Lower House of parliament on Monday afternoon laying out his government's economic agenda. But it was not clear if this would contain any new measures or any revisions of previously announced policy.

Brokers said that apart from watching for hints of any remedies for the falling stock market, the market would also seek clues to whether the government would revise the budget for the next fiscal year from April 1 by postponing a consumption tax rise or delaying the end of special income tax cuts.

Many fear that without such steps, Japan's fragile economic recovery could stall. Concern over an economic slowdown has been weighing down the market since the budget was approved by the cabinet in late December.

Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita on Monday attempted to calm such fears, telling a central bank branch managers' meeting that Japan's economy was still gradually recovering and that the strength of that recovery was growing gradually.

The key March Japanese government bond futures contract was up sharply at midday due to the plunge in share prices, on the assumption that a weak stock market means interest rates will have to stay at low levels.
